newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Coffee demand growth centred on E.Europe, Asia-ICO.
newsitem.headline: Coffee demand growth centred on E.Europe, Asia-ICO.

text.p: The liberalised or liberalising markets of Eastern Europe and the Far East hold the greatest prospects for future coffee consumption, the head of the International Coffee Organisation (ICO) said on Tuesday.
ICO executive director Celsius Lodder's remarks were in a speech delivered by the ICO's Robert Hagen at an international coffee seminar in Rio on Tuesday.
Japan has been the big success story of the last thirty years, with coffee consumption progressing from 500,000 60-kg bags in 1965 to 6.2 million in 1995, Lodder said.
Although there are clear signs of levelling off, a modest continuing rate of growth of 0.6 percent should still take consumption up to around 6.4 million by 2000.
In Poland, consumption per capita at 2.2 kg in 1994 is still substantially below its German neighbour, although it has increased to 1.4 million bags from only 300,000 in 1965.
Here the annual growth rate currently exceeds 11 percent, leading to predictions of total consumption of around 2.2 million by 2000, with substantial involvement in the market by Western roasters.
In Russia severe economic and distribution problems remain, together with a traditionally tea-oriented consumer.
Nevertheless, current high annual growth rates of nearly 12 percent are likely to continue, bringing consumption in 2000 up to around 2.7 million bags, with excellent prospects for further progress.
Lodder said he hoped this movement would be further stimulated by the promotional programme which the lCO's Promotion Fund intends to develop for this market later this year.
He said the most exciting long-term prospects are for consumption in China.

"Not only is there a continued drive towards economic liberalisation but it is estimated that around 100 million Chinese have the necessary purchasing power to drink coffee on a regular basis. Again this is a target market for action by the ICO Promotion Fund," Lodder said.

Although the country remains very much a tea drinking area the analogy with Japan - also traditionally a tea consumer - shows that this need not hinder the introduction of coffee too much, and that soluble is, initially, the probable key to the
market.

Possible growth rates are shown by movements from 1985, when net imports were about 10,000 bags to 1995, when they reached nearly 200,000. On this basis consumption should reach anywhere between 0.5 and 1 million bags by 2000, but it is more likely to be towards the upper end of this range.
With the success of educational/promotional campaigns and continued economic progress a target of five million bags by 2005 is by no means out of the question.

High growth rates can also be seen in other emerging markets such as the Middle East and North Africa. Net imports by Turkey doubled from 1985 to 1995 from 70,000 to 140,000 bags while in Israel growth in the same decade was even higher - from 200,000 to 450,000 bags. In Algeria net imports in 1994 reached 1.6 million compared with only 200,000 in 1965.
The outlook for consumption in producing countries is, not surprisingly in view of the diversity of conditions, somewhat mixed, Lodder said.

In Brazil, in spite of a decline from 8.1 million to seven million between 1965 and 1985 but recent increases in consumer purchasing power, greater emphasis on quality in marketing and considerable advances in the sophistication of roasters has led to a reversal of the trend, with consumption reaching around 11.0 million bags in 1995.
Based only on current growth projections of just over four percent per annum the trend indicates the possibility of reaching a level of around 13 million bags by 2000.
This projection of course might change, and it probably will, if the recently launched campaign by ABIC to reach 15m bags by 2000 is considered, Lodder said..

Another growth area is Indonesia, reflecting current growth patterns in the Far East. Here domestic consumption increased from 1.2 million to 2.2 million bags between 1985 and 1994, with the annual growth rate up to 2000 running at over eight percent annually. This implies consumption in 2000 of around 3.4 million bags.

India, currently consuming one million bags, will also be a country to look at. Changes to the marketing system and increased awareness of competition and need for promotion may lead to increases in line with trends elsewhere in Asia.

Adding up all these trends one can reach the conclusion that, by 2000, the world will be drinking not less than 108 million bags of coffee. It remains to be seen whether we will be able to face and overcome short and medium term constraints.
"Personally I am sure, more than that, I am convinced, that, through the enhancement of the quality of our product, we will reach this target sooner than expected.

But I must emphasise that the search for quality requires an improvement and updating of processing, at the farm and factory level, in other words accelerated technological and agricultural change," Lodder concluded.
-- Caroline Bulloch, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
